hero.name: Karthik
hero.who: a 22-year-old state-level badminton player in Hyderabad whose anxious mind keeps costing him matches

story.b: Karthik is a state-level badminton player in Hyderabad, training at a stadium in Gachibowli. Physically, he is in the best shape of his life. Mentally, he is a mess. The night before a big quarter-final, he lies awake replaying every mistake from his last match and imagining his father's face if he loses. In the match, he leads, then panics after one bad line call, smashes into the net and loses in three games. His coach suggests he try meditation. Karthik laughs. Meditation is for monks in the hills, he thinks, and it would make him soft. He wants a killer instinct, not calm. But he cannot deny that his own mind is beating him.

ask.q: Karthik thinks meditation will make him soft, yet his mind keeps costing him matches. What is the most sensible move?
o: Ignore his mind and simply train his body harder
Try a short, simple mind practice for a few weeks as an experiment
Accept that some players are just born anxious
ask.why: His body is already strong, so more training does not touch the real problem. Calling himself born anxious closes the door on change. A short experiment with a simple mind practice costs little and lets him test for himself whether it helps.

chapters.take: A strong body cannot win if an untrained mind keeps losing.

story.b: On the bus to training, Karthik decides to simply notice what his mind is doing. Within five minutes, he catches a stream of thoughts. What if I lose to Venkat on Saturday? Dad will be disappointed. My backhand is useless. The selectors will never pick me. He is amazed. The voice has been running all day, every day, and he never noticed it. He had assumed that voice was just him. As the bus crawls through traffic near the flyover, he quietly names each thought as it comes: worry, worry, judging, planning. Naming them does not stop them. But for the first time, Karthik feels a little distance between himself and the noise.

ask.q: Karthik's friend Imran gets angry at himself in traffic but does not know why. What should Karthik suggest first?
o: Notice and name the thoughts running through his mind as they come
Distract himself with loud music so he does not have to think
Argue back against every negative thought until it stops
ask.why: Distraction only covers the chatter for a while, and arguing with every thought keeps him trapped in it. Simply noticing and naming the thoughts creates a little space, which is the first step toward not being run by them.

chapters.take: Noticing the voice in your head is the first step to being free of it.

story.b: Karthik starts sitting for five minutes each morning on his hostel bed, before his roommates wake up. The instructions are simple: feel the breath, notice when the mind wanders, come back. On the first day, his mind wanders about thirty times. He thinks of breakfast, the coach, a video he saw, the Saturday match. He feels like he is failing. Then he remembers how training works. Each time he brings his attention back is like one rep in the gym. The wandering is not the failure. Coming back is the exercise. By the second week, he still wanders often, but he notices sooner. The practice is simple. It is not easy, and Karthik decides that is fine.

ask.q: Karthik's teammate tried meditating once, kept wandering and decided he is bad at it. What should Karthik tell him?
o: Sit for an hour next time to force his mind to stay still
Give up, since some people simply cannot meditate
Wandering is normal, and gently coming back is the actual exercise
ask.why: Forcing an hour only makes the struggle longer, and giving up assumes wandering means failure. Every return to the breath is like one rep, so a wandering mind is exactly where the training happens. Short, regular sessions build the skill.

chapters.take: A wandering mind is not failure. Coming back is the practice.

story.b: In a district tournament, Karthik leads 18 to 15 in the second game when the line judge calls his clear smash out. The old heat rises in his chest. Last season, a call like this made him shout at the umpire and earn a warning. This time, he notices the anger, almost as if watching it from one step away. He takes a slow breath while picking up the shuttle. The anger is still there, but it is not driving. He nods, walks back and focuses on the next serve. He wins the game 21 to 18. Afterwards his coach does not mention the score. He mentions the breath, which he noticed from the stands.

ask.q: Karthik's sister is furious about a rude message from a classmate. What should she do before replying?
o: Reply immediately while the anger is fresh and honest
Notice the anger, take a slow breath, then choose how to respond
Pretend she does not feel angry at all
ask.why: Replying in the heat of anger often leads to regret, and pretending the anger is not there only buries it. Noticing the feeling and pausing for a breath creates a gap, so she can choose a calmer, wiser response instead of reacting automatically.

chapters.take: A small pause between feeling and action lets you choose.

story.b: The state selection trials are two weeks away, and Karthik feels the old worry growing. He fears that if he stops worrying, he will stop caring. One evening, in his notebook, he draws two columns. In one, he writes what he can control: sleep by ten, footwork drills, smash practice, food, studying his opponents' old matches. In the other, what he cannot: the draw, the selectors' moods, his opponents' form, the line judges. He gives everything to the first column. Whenever a thought from the second column appears, he notices it and lets it go. Karthik trains harder than ever, yet sleeps better than he has in months.

ask.q: Karthik's friend worries constantly about an upcoming job interview. What approach fits the idea best?
o: Prepare fully for what she can control, and let go of what she cannot
Worry as much as possible, since worry shows she cares
Stop preparing so she does not feel any pressure
ask.why: Endless worry drains energy without improving the outcome, and dropping preparation gives up on the goal. Putting full effort into what she can control and letting go of the rest keeps her ambitious and far calmer.

chapters.take: Work hard on what you can control. Let go of the rest.

story.b: Venkat, a teammate and rival, keeps mocking Karthik's backhand in the dressing room. Karthik usually stews on it for hours. His coach suggests something odd: sit for a few minutes and silently wish good things to himself, to his family, and then to Venkat. Karthik thinks it sounds soft and silly. He tries it anyway, one night in the hostel. May you be well. May you play well. It feels fake at first, especially for Venkat. But after a week, the comments sting less. He stops stewing. One day he even praises Venkat's drop shot. Venkat looks surprised, and later he offers to practise doubles with Karthik.

ask.q: Karthik's cousin is constantly irritated by a cranky neighbour. What might help her own mood most?
o: Complain about the neighbour to everyone in the building
Avoid him completely and keep the anger to herself
Silently wish the neighbour well each day and notice how she feels
ask.why: Complaining keeps the irritation alive, and holding anger inside lets it sour her mood. Silently wishing the neighbour well may sound soft, but practising kindness can ease her own irritation and make daily life feel lighter.

chapters.take: Kindness can be practised, and it often helps you most.

story.b: Weeks later, Karthik plays the state selection trials. Before his first match, he sits on the bench for two minutes, eyes closed, feeling his breath. In the deciding game, a line call goes against him again. He notices the heat, breathes and plays the next point. He makes the state squad. That night, he does not lie awake replaying mistakes. He still wants to win as badly as ever. He still trains hard and hates losing. The difference is quieter. His mind no longer fights him. Venkat makes the squad too, and now they are doubles partners. Karthik's father, watching from the stands, says he has never seen his son look so calm.

chapters.take: A calmer mind did not soften his ambition. It sharpened it.
